title: Curated Synthetic Data Doesn’t Have to Collapse: A Theoretical Study of Generative Retraining with Pluralistic Preferences
claim: Curation with a single fixed reward collapses onto one mode; curation with multiple sampled rewards preserves diverse high-reward modes.
layout: 5 panels, 2x2 grid plus bottom strip; single vs pluralistic columns, color-coded
description: A five-panel figure with dashed borders. The top row, (a) single-preference curation and (b) pluralistic curation, shows data flowing left to right. Training images pass through a neural-net generator to sampled candidates, then to one curator (airplanes) in (a) or two curators (airplanes and dogs) in (b), and end in curated datasets. Reward legends sit below. The middle row shows the recursive retraining loop as a circular diagram with Retraining, Sampling and Curation stages. In (c), a blue loop with one curator ends in a red 'Mode Collapse' label above a grid of identical airplanes. In (d), a green loop with two curators ends in a green 'No Collapse' label above a grid of mixed airplanes, birds and dogs. Panel (e) at the bottom gives the stochastic reward sampling rule, Pr[r_i=r_1]=q and 1−q, with airplane and dog icons. The eye goes first to the contrasting red and green outcome grids.
caption: Overview of pluralistic curation. At each retraining step, the generative model samples candidates from its current distribution. A reward function is chosen at random $r_1$ with probability $q$, or $r_2$ with probability $1 - q$ and one candidate is selected. The model is then retrained to maximize the likelihood of this curated sample. Over time, this alternating selection drives the model toward a stable mixture over the distinct high-reward regions associated with $r_1$ and $r_2$, preventing mode collapse and preserving diversity.
abstract: Recursive retraining of generative models poses a critical representation challenge: when synthetic outputs are curated based on a fixed reward signal, the model tends to collapse onto a narrow set of outputs that over-optimize that objective. Prior work suggests that such collapse is unavoidable without adding real data into the mix. We revisit this conclusion from an alignment perspective and show that collapse can be mitigated through curation based on multiple reward functions. We formalize the dynamics of recursive training under heterogeneous preferences and prove that, under certain conditions, the model converges to a stable distribution that allocates probability mass across competing high-reward regions. The limiting distribution preserves diversity and provably satisfies a weighted Nash bargaining solution, offering a formal interpretation of value aggregation in synthetic retraining loops.
